stories.head: Spain high-speed train crash near Toledo kills at least 68
stories.say: At least 68 people died when a Renfe high-speed train ran into a stopped Iryo train near Urda in Toledo province on Wednesday, and Spain has begun three days of mourning.
stories.stand: A Renfe AVE hit the back of a stopped Iryo train on the Madrid to Seville line, Spain's second deadly rail crash this year.
body: At least 68 people were killed on Wednesday when two high-speed trains collided near Urda, in Toledo province, on the line between Madrid and Seville.
A Renfe AVE carrying 397 passengers ran into the back of an Iryo train carrying 147 people, which had stopped on the tracks. Two carriages left the line, and some came to rest down an embankment.

El Tiempo reported that a signalling failure had halted several trains and that the Atocha control centre then allowed the AVE to continue. Transport Minister Óscar Puente called that order inexplicable. The Guardia Civil and the rail accident commission questioned the operator.
Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez declared three days of official mourning, until 31 October. The crash came nine months after a collision near Adamuz in January killed 45 people.

stories.head: UN condemns US embargo on Cuba with weakest backing since 1995
stories.say: The UN General Assembly voted 130 to 17 on Wednesday to condemn the US embargo on Cuba, with 25 abstentions, as Germany and Italy declined to back the resolution.
stories.stand: The annual non-binding resolution passed again, but support fell to its lowest level since 1995 after a US lobbying push.
body: The UN General Assembly adopted its annual resolution against the US embargo on Cuba on Wednesday. It passed with 130 votes in favour, 17 against and 25 abstentions.
Support was the lowest since 1995. Germany and Italy abstained, and Colombia, Costa Rica and Ecuador were among those voting against. Euronews said more than 160 countries backed it last year.

US Ambassador Mike Waltz denied that Cuba was under a blockade and blamed the "corrupt communist regime" for its hardships. Cuban officials accused Washington of threatening countries with tariffs and visa curbs.
President Miguel Díaz-Canel called the US conduct gangster-like coercion. The resolution is not binding.

stories.head: Costa Rica's new mega-prison receives its first inmates
stories.say: Costa Rica has moved its first inmates into a new $35 million maximum-security prison for up to 5,100 people, built with help from El Salvador, as it fights organised crime.
stories.stand: The CACCO prison near San José can hold about a fifth of Costa Rica's inmates and is central to the government's tough line on crime.
body: Costa Rica has begun moving inmates into CACCO, a new maximum-security prison for organised crime near San José. The Justice Ministry shared images on Tuesday of 123 inmates.
The prison cost $35 million and can hold up to 5,100 people, about 20% of the country's prison population, according to Justice Minister Gabriel Aguilar. El Salvador helped with its design.
Aguilar said the first intake targets inmates who kept running criminal activity from prison. The prison is a symbol of President Laura Fernández's tough approach to crime.
Costa Rica recorded 873 homicides in 2025. Authorities blame most killings on disputes between drug-trafficking groups.

stories.head: Strike on Darfur market killed more than 100, rights group says
stories.say: A rights group says more than 100 people were killed in a strike on a market in Nyala, South Darfur, on Monday, while a doctors' network gives a much lower toll of 21.
stories.stand: Tolls for the strike in the RSF-held city vary widely, and an army-aligned force says it hit militia recruits.
body: A strike on a busy market in Nyala, the capital of South Darfur, on Monday killed more than 100 people and wounded 113, the rights group Emergency Lawyers said. It said many victims were women and children.
Other figures are far lower. The Sudan Doctors Network gave a preliminary toll of 21 dead. Médecins Sans Frontières said a hospital it supports received 36 bodies.

Witnesses described a drone strike as fighters gathered. A spokesman for the Special Operations Forces, which fight alongside the army, said a strike near Nyala killed more than 150 "militia recruits".
Nyala is held by the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, which have fought the army since April 2023.

stories.head: Up to 50,000 flee clashes in southern Ethiopia into Kenya
stories.say: Up to 50,000 people have crossed from southern Ethiopia into Kenya to escape clashes around Moyale, the UN refugee agency says, many of them women and children.
stories.stand: Fighting between Ethiopia's Somali and Oromia regional forces has driven a fast-rising number of people into Kenya's Marsabit County.
body: Up to 50,000 people have fled clashes in southern Ethiopia into Kenya, the UN refugee agency said on Wednesday, citing local border authorities. It had recorded 36,000 crossings on Tuesday.
AFP reported that the fighting involves forces of Ethiopia's Somali and Oromia regions. It began after a Somali regional flag was raised in Moyale, a city run jointly by the two regions.
Many arrivals are women and children. They are staying in schools, churches and with host families around Moyale in Kenya's Marsabit County.
Fatima Mohammed-Cole, the agency's representative in Kenya, warned the number could change quickly. Aid groups plan dry food rations for more than 15,000 people.

stories.head: Tanzania announces its first major gas discovery in a decade
stories.say: Tanzania's energy minister has announced an estimated 223 billion cubic feet of gas at the Mnazi Bay field, though the French operator has given a lower, more cautious figure.
stories.stand: The find at the Kasa-1X well could start producing as early as November, in a country that relies on gas for most of its power.
body: Energy Minister Juma Homera announced on Tuesday an estimated 223 billion cubic feet of natural gas at the Kasa-1X well in the Mnazi Bay area. Africanews called it Tanzania's first major gas discovery in a decade.

The block is run by French company Maurel & Prom, which holds 60%, with the state-owned Tanzania Petroleum Development Corporation. The operator put the volume at about 200 billion cubic feet and has not classified it as a reserve.
Production from the well could start as early as November. Natural gas already supplies nearly 80% of Tanzania's electricity.

stories.head: South Sudan independence figure Joseph Lagu dies
stories.say: Joseph Lagu, who led the Anyanya rebels in Sudan's first civil war and signed the 1972 peace deal, has died in Juba, and President Salva Kiir has declared national mourning.
stories.stand: The former rebel leader and Sudanese vice-president helped win autonomy for the south in 1972 and lived to see South Sudan's independence.
body: Joseph Lagu, a founding figure of South Sudan's struggle for independence, has died in Juba. President Salva Kiir announced his death and declared national mourning until his burial.
Lagu led the Anyanya rebel movement in Sudan's first civil war. In 1972 he signed the Addis Ababa Agreement, which ended the war and gave the south regional autonomy.
He later served as Sudan's second vice-president and as its ambassador to the UN from 1990 to 1992. Kiir, who served under his command, said Lagu lived to see the birth of the country he fought for.
Flags will fly at half-mast across South Sudan and at its missions abroad.

stories.head: Taiwan warns of 'obvious' threat from more than 50 Chinese vessels
stories.say: Taiwan's security chief Joseph Wu says more than 50 Chinese navy and official vessels are operating from southern Japan to the Philippines, an obvious threat to all three.
stories.stand: Taiwan published a map showing 53 Chinese ships, including the carrier Liaoning's group, spread across waters near Japan, Taiwan and the Philippines.
body: Joseph Wu, secretary-general of Taiwan's National Security Council, said on Wednesday that more than 50 Chinese navy and official vessels were operating across a wide stretch of sea. He called the simultaneous threat to Taiwan, Japan and the Philippines obvious.
A map he posted showed 53 ships, 34 of them warships. The aircraft carrier Liaoning and its group were east of the Philippines, with other formations off Taiwan and southern Japan.

Defence Minister Wellington Koo said Taiwan was not happy with efforts to project deterrence. China's defence ministry said earlier this month that the Liaoning was on routine training not aimed at any country.

stories.say: Cyclone Arnab has killed at least three people in Andhra Pradesh, India's disaster response force says, after more than 180,000 people were evacuated there and in Odisha.
stories.stand: The storm damaged homes, crops and power lines in Andhra Pradesh and shut three airports, while Odisha reported no deaths.
body: At least three people have been killed after Cyclone Arnab struck India's east coast, a National Disaster Response Force official said. The deaths were in Andhra Pradesh, where the storm made landfall.
More than 180,000 people were evacuated in Andhra Pradesh and Odisha. Operations at three Andhra Pradesh airports were suspended.

Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister N Chandrababu Naidu wrote to Home Minister Amit Shah about damage to homes, crops and power supplies. Odisha Chief Minister Mohan Charan Majhi said his state had recorded no deaths.
The storm weakened after landfall, but heavy rain was forecast for neighbouring states.

stories.say: Serbian police shot dead a teenage knife attacker who wounded an officer guarding the Israeli embassy in Belgrade early on Wednesday, in what officials call a terrorist attack.
stories.stand: Serbia raised its terrorism threat level to the highest after a minor described as an Islamic State supporter attacked the embassy guard.
body: An attacker armed with two knives was shot dead after wounding a police officer guarding the Israeli embassy in Belgrade, shortly after midnight on Wednesday. The officer suffered a slight wound to the face.
Interior Minister Ivica Dacic called it a terrorist attack. He said the attacker was a minor from the town of Sabac, known to security services as an Islamic State supporter.
Serbia raised its terrorism threat level to the highest. Israel's foreign ministry said embassy staff were not hurt.
In June 2024, a man with a crossbow wounded an officer guarding the same embassy before being shot dead.

stories.head: EU drops 'associate membership' offer to Canada before summit
stories.say: EU countries led by Germany have removed associate membership for Canada from a joint summit declaration, replacing it with a pledge of ever closer association.
stories.stand: Germany objected to a term with no legal basis in EU treaties as Mark Carney prepared to host EU leaders in Montreal.
body: The idea of associate EU membership for Canada has been dropped from a joint declaration due at an EU-Canada summit in Montreal, which starts on Thursday.
Ursula von der Leyen floated the idea last month. Diplomats said Germany led objections, saying the concept had no legal status. Euronews reported that France, Italy and Greece also raised concerns.
The text now commits both sides to ever closer association. Reuters reported it also includes a study on Canadian gas exports to Europe and plans for subsea cables.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said specific names or nomenclature did not matter.

stories.stand: The former comedian denies rape and sexual assault charges brought by six women over the period 1999 to 2009.
body: Russell Brand, 51, began giving evidence in his own defence at Southwark Crown Court in London on Wednesday 28 October.
He denies three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one charge of attempted indecent assault. The allegations were made by six women and cover 1999 to 2009.

He said the 2023 documentary and press reports about him had been devastating, and that friends and colleagues had abandoned him. The trial continues.

stories.stand: The defendant accepts carrying out the attack on a London-bound train last November but denies intending to kill.
body: The trial of Anthony Williams, 33, over a mass stabbing on an LNER train opened at Cambridge Crown Court on Wednesday 28 October.
Ten people were stabbed on the London-bound service on 1 November 2025. The train made an emergency stop at Huntingdon in Cambridgeshire, and the attack lasted about five minutes.
Williams accepts he carried out the train attack but denies 14 counts of attempted murder. Some counts relate to people allegedly stabbed in Peterborough and London around the same time.
Prosecutor Christopher Paxton KC said Williams brought terror to the service. He told jurors a crew member would say Williams asked a passenger whether they wanted to die.

stories.say: A jury at Southwark Crown Court convicted Tommy Robinson by a ten to two majority on Wednesday of harassing two journalists, after messages, calls and posts in 2024.
stories.stand: Stephen Yaxley-Lennon was convicted of two counts of harassment causing fear of violence and will be sentenced in December.
body: Tommy Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, was found guilty on Wednesday of two counts of harassment causing fear of violence.
The jury at Southwark Crown Court reached its verdicts by a 10-2 majority. He was granted bail and is due to be sentenced on 16 December, RTÉ reported.

The charges related to two Daily Mail journalists in August 2024, after a story about him during the riots that followed the Southport killings. Prosecutors said he hired private investigators to find their home addresses.
The Metropolitan Police said the journalists feared for their safety and their families. Robinson had argued he only wanted a photo of his former wife removed.

stories.say: A Belfast judge ruled on Wednesday that Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant acted lawfully in banning the Drumcree parade, though he called it highly regrettable.
stories.stand: Mr Justice Scoffield dismissed an Orange Order member's judicial review of the ban, and an appeal is expected.
body: Mr Justice Scoffield dismissed a judicial review at the High Court in Belfast on Wednesday 28 October. It had been brought by a member of the Orange Order.
He found that Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant's decision to ban the Drumcree parade was lawful, but said it was highly regrettable it had been needed.

The Parades Commission had approved the parade's traditional route along the mainly nationalist Garvaghy Road for the first time in almost 30 years. Sir Chris banned it on 9 October after talks failed.
The court heard police intelligence that dissidents may have mounted gun attacks on officers if a path had been cleared. An appeal is expected.

stories.stand: Army bomb disposal officers carried out a controlled explosion after the alert during a Halloween fun fair nearby.
body: A suspicious package delivered to a hotel in the Waterside area of Londonderry contained a viable explosive device, the PSNI said on Wednesday.
The alert began at 3.20pm on Tuesday 27 October, while a Halloween fun fair was taking place nearby. The hotel and several neighbouring properties were evacuated.
Army ammunition technical officers carried out a controlled explosion, and the remains were taken for forensic examination. Police called it a reckless and targeted attack.
Chief Superintendent Gillian Kearney said dissident republicans may be responsible but police had an open mind. Justice Minister Naomi Long condemned the attack. No arrests have been reported.

stories.say: Seven people accused of damaging Donald Trump's Turnberry golf resort in Ayrshire will go on trial in February 2028, a judge at the High Court in Glasgow decided on Wednesday.
stories.stand: Prosecutors say the alleged vandalism in March 2025 was aggravated by a terrorist connection; six have pleaded not guilty.
body: Lord Arthurson set a 15-day trial at the High Court in Glasgow from 14 February 2028, at a virtual hearing on Wednesday. A preliminary hearing is due in March 2027.
The seven accused are charged over damage at the Trump Turnberry resort in South Ayrshire on 8 March 2025. Prosecutors say the offence was aggravated by a terrorist connection.
The alleged damage includes dug-up turf, weedkiller sprayed on greens, painted slogans and a broken sprinkler system that caused flooding.
Not guilty pleas were entered for six of the accused. A plea was not recorded for Ricky Southall, whose lawyer needed more time. All seven remain on bail.

body: Marcin Buryta, 32, was found guilty of murder at Winchester Crown Court on Tuesday 27 October. He is due to be sentenced on Thursday 29 October.

The gun was a Glock pistol with parts made by 3D printing. Police also found two more firearms, a loaded crossbow, a machete and knives. Buryta had admitted firearms and ammunition charges.
Jurors rejected his claim that he feared for his life. Detective Chief Inspector Clair Trueman described him as obsessed with weapons.

body: Chancellor John Healey delivered his first Budget on Wednesday 28 October. Its centrepiece is a £2.6bn energy support package, including a one-off £100 payment for up to 20 million households.

According to GOV.UK, the payment goes to households in council tax bands A to D in England from January 2027. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland get extra funding to use as they choose. VAT stays off household electricity until mid-2027.
City AM reported that the banking surcharge doubles to 6% for 15 months, raising an expected £1.5bn. Landlords and savers also face higher taxes, and the fuel duty freeze is extended.
The Office for Budget Responsibility cut next year's growth forecast from 1.6% to 1%. It said real household disposable income would shrink in 2027. Kemi Badenoch said the Budget was not good enough.

body: Conservative activists James O'Keefe and Cam Higby were charged on Wednesday with felony unlawful voting and identity theft. Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty announced the charges.

Prosecutors say the men wore costumes during Minnesota's August 11 primary and gave poll workers the names of registered voters without their permission. They were starting the vouching process, which lets a registered voter vouch for someone without proof of address.

Poll workers grew suspicious and reported them. The men did not sign the required oath, but Moriarty said giving false names and starting the process was enough for charges. They filmed the encounters for a YouTube video.
O'Keefe Media Group said the men presented an intentionally extreme scenario to expose flaws in the system. Neither man has entered a plea.

body: US District Judge David Carter on Wednesday rejected a Trump administration request to make California set aside mail ballots from about 20,000 registered voters. The Justice Department says they are likely not US citizens.

Carter said the request ran against longstanding constitutional principles giving states authority over their elections. CBS News reported he called the verification method vague and said he could not conclude the process was credible.

According to Reuters, via Daily Maverick, the department quickly appealed to the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals. California says its safeguards are robust and that the department relied on suspect data.
Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles, said the department was not asking to void or cancel any ballots. The midterm elections are on 3 November.

His open letter first called him Brazil's elected president, then was replaced by a version calling him its leader. He alleged electoral fraud but offered no evidence, and said he had not fled but refused political persecution.

He thanked Argentine President Javier Milei and Donald Trump, whose administration granted his family visas. Lula called his departure shameful.

body: Cuauhtémoc Cárdenas died on Wednesday in Mexico City aged 92, according to Infobae. President Claudia Sheinbaum announced his death, the Associated Press reported.
The son of President Lázaro Cárdenas, he was governor of Michoacán before breaking with the PRI. The AP said his 1988 presidential defeat is widely seen as the result of electoral fraud.
He co-founded the Party of the Democratic Revolution in 1989 and ran for president again in 1994 and 2000. In 1997 he became Mexico City's first elected head of government. He left the party in 2014.
Sheinbaum called him a man of firm principles. Former presidents Vicente Fox and Andrés Manuel López Obrador also paid tribute.

body: All Spanish parties except Vox cancelled pre-campaign events after Wednesday's high-speed train crash at Urda, in Toledo province, killed 68 people, Ara reported. The general election is on 29 November.

Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez visited the site and said it was not acceptable for Spain to suffer two such accidents in one year. In January, 46 people died in a crash in southern Spain. Three days of mourning began on Thursday.

Popular Party leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo demanded a full investigation, and his party cancelled its events for the day. Vox leader Santiago Abascal kept campaigning, blamed Sánchez and called for Transport Minister Óscar Puente to resign.
Puente said a central command order letting a train resume at normal speed was inexplicable. The Associated Press said polls show Sánchez's Socialists facing an uphill battle.

stories.say: The Federal Reserve kept its key rate in a range of 3.75 to 4 percent on Wednesday, but two policymakers, Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack, wanted another quarter-point rise.
stories.stand: The US central bank paused after its September hike, with Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack dissenting in favour of a quarter-point increase.
body: The US Federal Reserve held its benchmark interest rate in a range of 3.75% to 4% on Wednesday, six days before the midterm elections. It had raised rates in September, its first increase since 2023.
The vote was 10-2, according to Fortune. Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack both wanted a quarter-point rise. Yahoo Finance said it was Cook's first ever dissent.
US consumer prices rose 3.7% in the year to September, and core inflation was 2.6%. Both figures were above economists' expectations, CBS News reported.

The Fed's statement said more information would help it decide its policy stance. Chair Kevin Warsh, who replaced Jerome Powell in May, has not signalled the next move. Many economists expect a rise in December.

stories.head: Bank of Canada raises rates to 2.5% in first hike since 2023
stories.say: The Bank of Canada raised its key rate by a quarter point to 2.5 percent on Wednesday, its first increase since 2023, saying high energy prices risk feeding wider inflation.
stories.stand: Governor Tiff Macklem said high energy prices risked spreading into wider inflation, and warned that further increases could follow.
body: The Bank of Canada raised its key interest rate from 2.25% to 2.5% on Wednesday. It was the bank's first increase since July 2023.
Governor Tiff Macklem said the move aimed to stop high energy prices spreading into broader inflation. He said the rate might need to rise further, but the bank would proceed carefully.
Canadian inflation reached 3.2% in September, CP24 reported. The bank expects it to be about 3.5% at the end of 2026 and to return close to 2% by mid-2028.
It forecasts growth of 1% in 2026 and 2% in both 2027 and 2028. New US tariffs are expected to slow the economy in the fourth quarter.

body: The Office for Budget Responsibility cut its UK growth forecast for 2027 to 1%, alongside John Healey's first Budget on Wednesday. Trustnet and City AM said the previous forecast was 1.6%.
The Chancellor's headroom against his main fiscal rule has fallen to £15bn, down from £23.6bn in the spring. AOL reported that debt interest costs were £14bn higher than expected.

The money helps fund a £100 payment to about 20 million households in council tax bands A to D this winter, costing £2.6bn, Trustnet reported.

stories.head: European gas price tops €100 for first time since 2022
stories.say: Europe's benchmark gas price rose above one hundred euros per megawatt hour on Wednesday for the first time since 2022, as the Iran war disrupts supplies of liquefied gas.
stories.stand: The Dutch benchmark has roughly tripled since the Iran war began, and the EU's energy commissioner warned of another energy crisis.
body: The front-month Dutch TTF contract, Europe's benchmark gas price, reached €100.37 per megawatt hour on Wednesday afternoon. It was the first time above €100 since December 2022, Yahoo Finance reported.

The price was about €32 before the Iran war began in late February. Disruption to liquefied natural gas shipments, mainly from Qatar, has cut supplies. ING said QatarEnergy has reportedly extended force majeure for several buyers until the end of the year.
EU Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen said Europe faces another energy crisis. EU gas storage was about 75% full, short of the usual 90% target for 1 November.
ING said fertiliser maker Yara has curtailed European ammonia production because of high gas prices.

body: A Canadian government official said trade talks with the US had made limited progress, Reuters reported on Wednesday. Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canada would pursue deals that serve both countries, but was not in that position yet.
Talks have focused on US Section 232 tariffs of up to 50% on Canadian steel and 25% on cars, according to Reuters. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has held talks with Canadian counterparts.

A revised list of 50% US tariffs on Canadian goods takes effect on 30 October. Container News said some plywood, paper and packaging goods are removed, and more than 100 product categories added, including some paints and carpets.
CTV News, via BNN Bloomberg, reported that Canadian cabinet ministers are deeply sceptical of a broad deal. Carney has named car tariffs as one of his red lines.

body: Poundland's directors were preparing to appoint AlixPartners as administrators through a High Court filing, City AM reported on Wednesday. The chain has about 600 stores and nearly 12,000 staff.

Owner Gordon Brothers, which bought Poundland from Pepco Group for less than £1 last year, rejected a takeover offer from Ireland's Martin Property Group. That firm had not agreed to repay a £30m loan up front.

Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds has asked an adviser to look into the situation, Retail Insight Network reported, citing the Financial Times. Three directors advising on the sale resigned after the offer was rejected.

The union Usdaw warned of 11,000 redundancies before Christmas. Lidl, Iceland, B&M, The Range and Poundstretcher are among those interested in stores, City AM said. AlixPartners and Gordon Brothers declined to comment.

The engines are for single-aisle passenger aircraft and military planes. FlightGlobal said Rolls-Royce's UltraFan is its proposed single-aisle engine candidate.

body: The Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile has found its first dwarf planet candidate. The object, provisionally named 2026 ED138, was announced on 27 October through the Minor Planet Center.

Matthew Holman of the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian spotted it on 13 October using search software built with Kevin Napier. Mario Jurić of the University of Washington found further observations in Rubin's data.
Rubin recorded the object 30 times on 20 nights between 4 March and 11 July 2026. Older Dark Energy Camera images go back to 2016.

It is about 46 au from the Sun, beyond Pluto's average of 40 au, on an orbit tilted about 25 degrees. Its size depends on how reflective it is, so infrared observations are needed to confirm its size and status.

stories.say: United Launch Alliance says its Vulcan rocket will fly again on 13 November, carrying Amazon internet satellites, after months grounded by a booster nozzle failure.
body: United Launch Alliance (ULA) says its Vulcan rocket will return to flight on Friday 13 November. The mission will carry satellites for Amazon's Leo internet network.
Spaceflight Now reported the rocket will carry 40 satellites from Cape Canaveral and fly with 6 solid rocket boosters for the first time.
Vulcan has been grounded since a nozzle failed on a Northrop Grumman-built booster during the Space Force's USSF-87 mission on 12 February. The launch still reached orbit.

ULA said an investigation identified several potential contributors, which were addressed with design and process changes. The flight will use a redesigned nozzle. It is unclear when Vulcan will fly military missions again.

body: Caltech has named Reid Wiseman, commander of NASA's Artemis II Moon mission, as deputy director of the Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL). Caltech manages JPL for NASA.
He will also be a Caltech associate vice president. The appointment takes effect on 30 November 2026.
Wiseman will oversee JPL operations and mission execution and act as the laboratory's main contact for national security programmes.

A retired US Navy captain and test pilot, he joined NASA's astronaut corps in 2009 and was chief astronaut from 2020 to 2022. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said Wiseman had spent his career at the edge of what is possible.

stories.stand: A Defense Intelligence Agency report includes a 2024 satellite photo of the secretive reusable craft docked to another satellite.
stories.say: A US Defense Intelligence Agency report includes the clearest picture yet of China's secretive Shenlong spaceplane, photographed in orbit in 2024 by a commercial satellite.
body: The US Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA) has published a photo of China's reusable Shenlong spaceplane in orbit. It appeared in a report released on Monday 26 October.

Space.com and Live Science said the image was taken in 2024 by a satellite from the company Vantor, formerly Maxar. Space.com said it shows Shenlong docked to an unidentified satellite with its payload bay doors open.
Live Science described it as the first clear image of the craft released publicly. Shenlong is on its fourth mission, which launched in February 2026.
China has said only that the craft tests technologies for affordable round trips to space for peaceful use. The DIA report says China is developing weapons to target satellites.

stories.head: Canadian astronaut set for first spacewalk to fit new station solar array
stories.stand: Joshua Kutryk and NASA's Anil Menon are due outside the ISS on Thursday to install a roll-out solar array.
stories.say: Canada's Joshua Kutryk and NASA's Anil Menon are due to leave the space station on Thursday for a spacewalk of about six hours and 45 minutes to fit a new solar array.
body: Joshua Kutryk of the Canadian Space Agency is due to make his first spacewalk on Thursday 29 October, with NASA's Anil Menon. Space.com said it will be Canada's first spacewalk in 7 years.
The pair are due to leave the International Space Station at about 8am EDT, 12:00 GMT, for about 6 hours 45 minutes. They will install a new roll-out solar array over older, ageing panels.
A second spacewalk on 5 November is planned to fit the final array. Space.com reported that, once all 8 are working, station power should rise from 160 to about 215 kilowatts.
Menon has made 3 previous spacewalks. Kutryk arrived at the station on a SpaceX Crew Dragon launched on 1 October.

stories.head: Physicists use hidden memory in a liquid to extract extra work from a bead
stories.stand: A Konstanz team says a Maxwell's demon-style feedback scheme gained up to 3 times the usual work limit by exploiting a fluid's memory.
stories.say: Physicists in Germany say they extracted up to three times the expected work from a tiny glass bead by exploiting hidden memory in the liquid around it.
body: Researchers at the University of Konstanz say they have extracted extra energy from a microscopic system by using information hidden in its surroundings. The study appeared in Nature Physics, ScienceAlert reported.
The team, including Clemens Bechinger, trapped a glass bead with a laser in a liquid containing micelles. These form a network that keeps traces of the bead's past movement.
By measuring the bead's position twice, about 1 second apart, and adjusting the trap, they extracted up to 3 times the work limit of a similar system without memory, under certain conditions.
The work echoes Maxwell's demon, an 1867 thought experiment. It does not break the second law of thermodynamics. It is a laboratory demonstration, not a working machine.

stories.stand: Polish physicists say lithium fluoride detectors in mannequins on Orion offer a simpler way to track astronauts' radiation dose.
stories.say: Physicists in Kraków say tiny lithium fluoride crystals flown on Artemis I measured radiation near the Moon, and could become a simpler dosimeter for astronauts.
body: Researchers at the Institute of Nuclear Physics of the Polish Academy of Sciences in Kraków have analysed radiation data from NASA's uncrewed Artemis I flight around the Moon in 2022.

Their lithium fluoride crystals, only millimetres across, rode inside two human-shaped mannequins on the Orion spacecraft. Particle tracks are read under a microscope, without the chemical etching plastic detectors need.
ScienceDaily reported that radiation near the Moon was higher than in low Earth orbit, but by less than might be expected. Doses were spread almost evenly through the mannequins.
The study, led by Paweł Bilski, appeared in Radiation Measurements. Universe Today noted calibration challenges remain at high energies.

stories.head: Black holes could split in two only at extreme spin, physicists calculate
stories.stand: A Physical Review D study suggests a black hole spinning near its maximum rate might divide, the reverse of a merger.
stories.say: Physicists say a black hole might be able to split into two, the reverse of a merger, but only if it spins at close to the fastest rate possible.
body: A study published on 22 October in Physical Review D suggests a single black hole might split into two, Space.com reported.
Splitting would lower entropy, which thermodynamics strongly disfavours. The team looked for conditions where that limit could be avoided, and found very rapid rotation was one.

Once the two black holes must also move apart rather than fall back together, the window largely closes, except for black holes spinning near their maximum rate. A split is likelier when one piece is much smaller.
Francesco Sannino of the University of Naples Federico II said the chance depends on how gravity behaves beyond Einstein's theory. No probability has yet been calculated.

stories.head: Jumping spiders catch up on lost REM-like sleep, study finds
stories.stand: Bonn researchers say disturbed Portia fimbriata spiders showed about 80% more REM-like sleep the next night.
stories.say: Researchers in Bonn say jumping spiders kept awake at night showed about 80 percent more REM-like sleep the following night, the first such rebound seen in an invertebrate.
body: Researchers at the University of Bonn say jumping spiders show two distinct sleep stages, including one that resembles REM sleep. The study was published in PNAS.
The spider studied, Portia fimbriata, is an Australian species. During REM-like bouts at night its limbs twitched and its retinas moved.

When the team disturbed the spiders at night, they showed about 80% more REM-like sleep behaviour the following night, ScienceAlert reported. The researchers call this the first demonstration of REM rebound in an invertebrate.
Sleep was identified from behaviour, not brain activity. Nadja Geiger and Daniela C. Rößler led the work, and the researchers caution it does not show whether spiders dream.

body: Scientists have described Gerrothorax maritimus, an armoured amphibian from the Late Triassic, about 237 million years ago. They say it is the first known to have lived only in the sea.
The 2 fossils were found in Guizhou province, China, in rock that formed far from land. Strontium in the bones matched Late Triassic seawater. The study appeared in Nature Ecology & Evolution.
The more complete specimen is about 73.7 cm long. Researchers think it was a flat, bottom-dwelling suction feeder.
None of the more than 8,000 living amphibian species is known to live fully in the sea. Ryosuke Motani of UC Davis said the animal was unusual because it was big.

stories.stand: Paludohadros proudlovii, found in 2001, lived in swampy southern England about 125 million years ago.
stories.say: A plant-eating dinosaur dug up in Surrey in 2001 has been named as a new species, Paludohadros proudlovii, after a brickworks manager who died aged 35.
body: The Natural History Museum says a dinosaur found at a Surrey brickworks in 2001 is a new genus and species. It has been named Paludohadros proudlovii.
The iguanodontian, a plant-eater with thumb spikes, lived about 125 million years ago in swampy lowlands. It was about 5 metres long and weighed 1.5 to 2 tonnes, roughly the size of a rhino.
The bones were not fully developed, so it was probably a juvenile. The name honours Will Proudlove, manager of the brick factory, who died aged 35 shortly before the excavation.
It was found about 100 metres from Baryonyx walkeri. The study, led by Ricardo Sacamoto with Professor Susannah Maidment, was published in the Journal of Systematic Palaeontology.

stories.say: Robert F. Kennedy Jr. issued a draft policy on Wednesday letting compounding pharmacies make six unapproved wellness peptides, a move FDA scientists had opposed, according to AP.
stories.stand: The US health secretary's draft policy covers BPC-157 and five other injectable peptides the FDA has not approved.
body: US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. filed a draft policy on Wednesday that would let compounding pharmacies prepare 6 peptides the FDA has not approved, CBS News reported.

The peptides are BPC-157, Epitalon, KPV, MOTS-c, Semax and TB-500. They are promoted in the wellness industry for muscle building, injury healing and energy. HHS said it did not intend to act against licensed pharmacies or doctors that compound them.

The policy requires patient-specific prescriptions, ingredients from FDA-registered makers, quality testing and reports of serious side effects. An HHS spokesperson said it does not grant FDA approval or establish safety and effectiveness.
According to AP, most FDA scientific staff opposed the plan. In 2023 the FDA put BPC-157 and TB-500 on its do-not-compound list. Public comment runs from Friday until 13 November, CBS reported.

stories.head: Lilly's retatrutide beats Ozempic in head-to-head diabetes trial
stories.say: Eli Lilly says its experimental drug retatrutide cut blood sugar more than Ozempic over 80 weeks and roughly doubled weight loss, though more patients quit over side effects.
stories.stand: Topline phase 3 results show about 20% weight loss on retatrutide against about 9% on Novo Nordisk's Ozempic.
body: Eli Lilly reported topline results on Wednesday from a phase 3 trial comparing retatrutide with Novo Nordisk's Ozempic in adults with type 2 diabetes. Patients were treated for 80 weeks.
Both retatrutide doses lowered A1C, a measure of blood sugar, by about 2.2 percentage points. Ozempic at its highest approved dose lowered it by about 1.8 points.
Patients on retatrutide lost about 20% of their body weight on average, compared with about 9% on Ozempic. Side effects such as constipation and vomiting were more common on retatrutide.
About 8% of patients on the higher retatrutide dose stopped because of side effects, against about 3% on Ozempic. The drug is not approved, and Lilly plans to publish full data.

stories.head: Anorexia and bulimia cases up 71% since 1990, global study finds
stories.say: About 18.1 million people had anorexia or bulimia in 2023, a global study in JAMA Psychiatry estimates, with Australia recording the highest national rate of any country.
stories.stand: The Global Burden of Disease analysis says cases rose 71% between 1990 and 2023 and will keep rising to 2050.
body: Cases of anorexia and bulimia nervosa rose 71% worldwide between 1990 and 2023, according to a Global Burden of Disease study published in JAMA Psychiatry.
The study estimates 18.1 million people had one of the two disorders in 2023: 3.92 million with anorexia and 14.2 million with bulimia. About 41% of cases were in people aged 10 to 24.
Australia had the highest national rate, at 1,026.5 per 100,000 people. Senior author Damian Santomauro, of the University of Queensland, told ABC News the survey methods may partly explain this.
The largest relative increases were in East Asia, South Asia and South-East Asia. The study covers 204 countries and forecasts 21.8 million cases by 2050. It excludes other eating disorders.

stories.say: Boston University researchers estimate about three in four former NFL players who died between 2008 and 2023 had the brain disease CTE, after adjusting for bias among brain donors.
stories.stand: The JAMA Network Open study found CTE in nearly 94% of donated brains and corrected for selection bias.
body: Researchers led by Boston University estimate that 75% of former NFL players who died between 2008 and 2023 had chronic traumatic encephalopathy, or CTE. The study was published on Wednesday in JAMA Network Open.

Nearly 94% of brains donated by former players showed CTE. Because players with symptoms were more likely to donate, the team compared donors with players who did not donate, using national death records.
Lead author Julia Gallini called the estimate concerning. CTE is linked to repeated head impacts and can only be confirmed after death.
The estimate does not apply to living players or to college and youth football. The NFL said it keeps working to make the game safer.

stories.stand: The CDC's 2026 antimicrobial resistance report covers 19 bacterial and fungal threats.
body: The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention published its 2026 Antimicrobial Resistance Threats Report on Tuesday. It covers 19 drug-resistant bacteria and fungi.
The CDC estimates these germs cause about 9.7 million infections and 50,800 deaths a year in the US.

body: A team at Fujita Health University in Aichi Prefecture has applied for approval to run Japan's first clinical study of uterus transplants, the university said on Wednesday.
The plan, submitted to the university's review committee on Monday, covers 3 women in their 20s and 30s who were born without a uterus and want to give birth.

stories.say: More than three in four European pilots surveyed had a microsleep at the controls in the previous four weeks, the European Cockpit Association says, and few trust fatigue reporting.
stories.stand: The survey of 7,200 pilots in 32 countries found only 12% trusted their fatigue reporting system.
body: A survey of 7,200 pilots in 32 countries, published by the European Cockpit Association, found more than 76% had at least one microsleep on the flight deck in the previous four weeks. It was carried out by consultancy Baines Simmons.
Euronews reported that 82% of pilots knew how to file a fatigue report but only 12% trusted the system. Fear of management's reaction was the most common reason for not reporting.
Fox News reported that 24.2% said they do not report fatigue and fly anyway. Travel Radar said pilots at Irish and Maltese airlines reported the highest fatigue levels.
ECA board director Coen George said fatigue goes unreported when pilots fear career consequences. EASA named aircrew fatigue as a consistent safety concern in June.

stories.say: Oxford researchers found 12 blood proteins linked to prostate cancer diagnosed more than 15 years later, though they say the findings are not yet ready to be used as a screening test.
stories.stand: The study in European Urology compared stored blood from 982 men who developed the cancer with 1,573 who did not.
body: Researchers at Oxford Population Health have linked proteins in men's blood to prostate cancer diagnosed more than 15 years later. The study was published in European Urology.
The team measured more than 6,000 proteins in blood samples from the EPIC study. They compared 982 men who later developed prostate cancer with 1,573 men who did not.

body: The COP31 presidency of Türkiye has released the Antalya Artificial Intelligence Pledge, a voluntary commitment for countries and organisations. It aims to use AI for climate action while addressing the energy and water demands of data centres.

COP31 runs from 9 to 20 November in Antalya.

stories.head: UK greenhouse gas emissions fell 1% in 2025, ONS estimates
stories.say: UK greenhouse gas emissions dipped by one per cent in 2025 to an estimated 473 million tonnes, the ONS says, as falls in manufacturing outweighed more household travel.
stories.stand: Provisional ONS figures show a small fall in UK emissions in 2025, driven by manufacturing, while household emissions edged up.
body: UK greenhouse gas emissions on a residence basis were an estimated 473 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (Mt CO2e) in 2025, the Office for National Statistics said on 28 October. That is 1.0% lower than 478 Mt in 2024 and 42.4% below 1990 levels.
Manufacturing had the largest fall of any industry, from 64 to 58 Mt, a drop of 9.7%.
Emissions from household spending rose 1.0%, from 124 to 125 Mt, led by a 2.6% increase in emissions from consumer travel. Households were the largest single source, at 26.5% of the total.
Emissions per unit of economic output were unchanged from 2024.

body: The 17th UN biodiversity conference, COP17, is scheduled to end in Yerevan, Armenia, on Friday 30 October. It is the first global review of progress under the 2022 Kunming-Montreal framework, which sets 23 targets for 2030.

stories.stand: Brussels has proposed a Climate Resilience Law to make EU states plan for extreme weather risks, based on a set warming trajectory.
body: The European Commission unveiled a Climate Resilience Framework on Tuesday 27 October, including a proposed European Climate Resilience Law. It sets a reference warming trajectory for risk assessments and planning.

Commission projections envisage 2C of global warming by 2050 and 3C by 2100, Euronews reported. Governments would have to say whether national, regional or local authorities are responsible for protecting citizens from climate disasters.

Climate commissioner Wopke Hoekstra estimated the damage from this summer's extreme weather at more than €100 billion. The Commission puts the cost of adapting Europe's infrastructure and economy at €70 billion a year, ESG Today reported.
A senior official said only about 25% of climate-exposed assets are insured. The plan contains no new money for households.

body: EU spending on oil imports averaged €27.6bn a month in the second quarter of 2026, up 55.8% from €17.7bn in 2025, Euronews reported. That is about €9.9bn more each month.

Experts quoted said costs are unlikely to fall soon.

body: Italian army specialists have removed about 250 First World War munitions, including artillery shells and mortar bombs, from the Dolomites in Trentino-Alto Adige, CNN reported, citing an army statement.
The work was carried out by the 2nd Engineer Regiment of the Julia Alpine brigade. It began in early August and the summer campaign ended on 16 October.
The Caré Alto and Lares glaciers have retreated quickly. Local authorities said low winter snowfall in 2025 and extreme summer temperatures in 2026 sped up melting.
The munitions date from the 1915-1918 'White War' between Italian and Austro-Hungarian forces. Hikers are told not to touch suspicious items and to report them.

stories.say: A new study finds a vast deep-water layer circling Antarctica has turned sharply saltier as sea ice shrinks, reversing decades of freshening, with possible effects on ocean heat.
stories.stand: Researchers report a sharp rise in salinity in Antarctic Intermediate Water, linked to sea ice loss, which carries heat and carbon around the world's oceans.
body: A new study documents a sharp rise in salinity in Antarctic Intermediate Water, a layer 2,300 to 4,000 feet deep that encircles Antarctica, Inside Climate News reported. The change reverses decades of freshening.
The researchers combined six independent datasets from 2004 to 2024, including Argo floats. As sea ice shrinks, less fresh water is released in the melt season, leaving the water saltier.
The layer carries heat, carbon, oxygen and nutrients north into the Indian, Pacific and Atlantic oceans. Co-author Bishakhdatta Gayen of the University of Melbourne said more monitoring is needed.
Michael Meredith of the British Antarctic Survey said it is unclear whether the shift is permanent, given the short record.

body: The leak website Distributed Denial of Secrets published data on more than 40,000 US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) employees on Wednesday, Reuters reported. The records cover staff at ICE, CBP, Homeland Security Investigations, CISA and other DHS agencies.
The files include names, phone numbers, email addresses and job titles. Email groups show which staff worked in special operations, surveillance, computer forensics and undercover work.

The site said the data came from a group calling itself Department of Peace, which claimed a hack of DHS in March. Co-founder Emma Best said it was taken from the Okta sign-on service DHS uses. Okta said it had no evidence its systems were compromised.
DHS said it was aware of a potential breach and was working to address it. Reuters could not verify the full trove but matched details for 6 named employees and confirmed phone numbers with 3.

stories.stand: The 14-inch and 16-inch models use M5 Pro or M5 Max chips, and pre-orders opened on Wednesday.
body: Apple announced a MacBook Pro with a touchscreen on Wednesday, the first Mac to support touch. It uses a tandem OLED panel that Apple calls the PROLED XDR display, in 14-inch and 16-inch sizes.

The notch is replaced by a Dynamic Island, which houses the webcam. There is no Face ID, GSMArena reported. The trackpad stays the main input, and macOS treats touches as clicks so existing apps work.
The machines use M5 Pro or M5 Max chips. Prices start at $2,899 for the 14-inch M5 Pro and $4,799 for the 16-inch M5 Max, before upgrades.

stories.stand: Google DeepMind says the model scored 88.2% on a vulnerability-finding test, with wider access promised but no date given.
body: Google announced Gemini 4 Carbon on Wednesday, calling it its strongest model. It follows Gemini 4 Argon, released two weeks earlier, and was presented by Koray Kavukcuoglu of Google DeepMind.

Google says Carbon scored 88.2% on SEC-bench Pro, which tests finding vulnerabilities, and 54.8% on the ExploitGym exploitation test. It also says the model ranks first on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, with a score of 59.

Access starts with a subset of cyber defenders and will widen to trusted partners. Google says broader availability is coming soon but gave no date. It says it is taking part in voluntary US government pre-release testing.
Introductory pricing is $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, according to Google.

The new Echo Dot doubles as a smart home hub and Wi-Fi extender. The Echo Show 16 is open for pre-order.

stories.stand: Critics say the terms would let Meta use publishers' content for AI, with deleting an account the only way to opt out.
body: Meta may delay new commercial terms for businesses on its platforms beyond 20 November, spokesperson Andy Stone said on X. The terms were first due on 30 October but were pushed back once after an outcry.

The terms would let Meta use automated software to access the websites of businesses that use Facebook, including for advertising and business products. Euronews reported they would cover articles, photos and videos, including paywalled content, and that the only way to opt out is to delete the account.

A coalition of Norwegian media groups, including NRK and Schibsted, has asked Oslo District Court for an injunction to stop the terms taking effect. Senator Adam Schiff has also urged Meta to withdraw the changes.
Stone said the terms are not about scraping news sites and that Meta will respect robots.txt preferences.

body: The US Department of Justice is asking how Nvidia's planned $12.9bn takeover of Hugging Face would affect competition in AI, Reuters reported on Wednesday, citing two people familiar with the matter.

Hugging Face is a platform where developers share open AI models and data. Officials want to know whether owning it would let Nvidia control a key distribution channel for AI, and whether it could be used to harm rivals.
The inquiry is part of a broader DOJ investigation into Nvidia's business practices that began under the Biden administration. Nvidia expects the deal to close in the first half of 2027.

Nvidia says Hugging Face will keep supporting rival processors, clouds and software. A DOJ spokesperson declined to discuss specific matters. Nvidia shares fell 1.7% on Wednesday after the report, Investing.com said.

stories.stand: Eight North Koreans and two Russians were named; US officials say such schemes help fund North Korea's weapons programmes.
body: The US Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control sanctioned 10 individuals and 1 entity on Wednesday over a scheme using disguised North Korean IT workers, SBS News reported. They are 8 North Korean nationals and 2 Russians.
OFAC says North Korean IT workers hide their identities to get jobs at companies in the US and allied countries. The regime keeps most of their wages, which officials say fund its weapons programmes.

According to Chainalysis, the entity is the First Financial and Technical Development Center, a North Korean-controlled body in Russia. Named facilitators include Russians Ilya Boykov and Vitold Obertas, accused of converting cryptocurrency earnings into cash.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the Treasury would keep using all available means to protect US companies. A UN panel estimates such operations earn North Korea $250m to $600m a year.

stories.stand: Chatbot providers must verify users' ages, offering at least one method that does not rely on government ID.
body: Governor Kathy Hochul signed a law on Wednesday restricting how AI chatbots interact with children in New York. It was sponsored by state Senator Kristen Gonzalez and Assemblymember Alex Bores.

For users under 18, or whose adult age is unconfirmed, chatbots may not pretend to be human or claim a romantic relationship. They also may not promote self-harm, suicide or eating disorders, or provide sexually explicit content.

Providers must verify ages, with at least one method not relying entirely on government ID, and delete age data afterwards. Residents can complain to the state attorney general, and penalties reach $25,000 per violation.
Hochul also signed a law requiring internet-connected baby monitors sold in New York to block unauthorised users, Engadget reported.

stories.stand: FCC Chairman Brendan Carr announced the plan, which would allow, but not require, prisons and jails to jam signals.
body: The US Federal Communications Commission will vote on 19 November on a rule letting state and local prisons and jails jam contraband mobile phones. Chairman Brendan Carr announced the plan in Little Rock, Arkansas.
Facilities could opt in but would not be required to use the technology. Supporters say it could stop inmates using smuggled phones to direct crimes from behind bars.
Jamming is currently illegal for non-federal users. The FCC has previously refused to allow it, citing the risk of interference with emergency and public safety communications, Engadget reported.

Under the proposal, facilities would have to show that jamming does not cause harmful interference outside designated areas. Carr appeared alongside Senator Tom Cotton and Arkansas Attorney General Tim Griffin.

body: Chinese chilli sauce maker Lao Gan Ma has denied online claims of mass layoffs linked to AI. Its hotline said the information was untrue, and HR staff said there had never been layoffs on the reported scale.

The claims followed remarks by executive Li Xin at a quality conference in Guizhou. Citing China Business Herald, Shanghai Daily said he described one production line with more than 600 pepper-sorting workers that kept 48 after an AI system began work.
The visual inspection system uses cameras to scan a conveyor belt every 0.3 seconds and remove damaged peppers. Li said 2025 revenue reached a record 5.4 billion yuan.

Some social media users threatened a boycott, and 36Kr reported that daily sales on one e-commerce platform fell after the rumour spread. The company has not said what happened to the other sorting workers.

Panettiere, 36, known for the TV series Heroes and Nashville, was found unresponsive in an apartment in Greenville on 16 August. ABC News reported that a coroner found an accidental overdose of several drugs, including fentanyl.

Police said the decision followed the medical examiner's determination and their own findings. A police spokeswoman, Sergeant Diana Munoz, said she could not comment on whether other agencies were investigating, ABC News reported.
ABC News also reported that her former fiancé, Wladimir Klitschko, was granted legal status by a California court in October to protect her property for their 11-year-old daughter, her sole heir.

stories.stand: The Budapest-born film-maker fled to England in 1956 and directed 27 feature films over six decades, plus episodes of The Wire and Breaking Bad.
body: The film director Peter Medak has died in Los Angeles at the age of 88. The UK Pulse reported that his family announced the death and that no cause was given.
Medak was born in Budapest in 1937 and fled to England during the 1956 Hungarian uprising. He worked in the British film industry before moving to Hollywood.
Over six decades he directed 27 feature films. They included The Ruling Class in 1972, which earned Peter O'Toole an Oscar nomination, the horror film The Changeling in 1980 and The Krays in 1990.

He also directed television, including episodes of Homicide: Life on the Street, The Wire, House and Breaking Bad. Yahoo Entertainment reported that he is survived by four children and five grandchildren.

body: The global girl group Katseye has added 11 dates in Asia, Australia and New Zealand to its Wildworld tour, with Live Nation promoting. The run begins at Yokohama Arena in Japan on 27 January.
It continues to Manila, Hong Kong, Seoul, Cebu, Singapore, Bangkok and Taipei, then Melbourne on 24 February and Sydney on 28 February. It ends at Spark Arena in Auckland on 5 March.
Presales begin on 4 November and general sale opens on 6 November. The tour began in Dublin on 1 September, with sold-out shows in Europe, the UK and North America.
The group's EP Wild debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard 200.

stories.head: Sarah J Maas fans flock to midnight launches for sixth ACOTAR novel
stories.say: Sarah J Maas's sixth A Court of Thorns and Roses novel, A Court of Splintered Harmony, went on sale on Tuesday, with fans gathering at midnight parties at bookshops across the US.
stories.stand: Bloomsbury publishes the romantasy series, and AFP reports that Maas has sold 75 million books in 40 languages.
body: A Court of Splintered Harmony, the sixth book in Sarah J Maas's A Court of Thorns and Roses series, was released on Tuesday. Fans attended midnight release parties at bookshops across the United States, AFP reported.

At The Ripped Bodice in Los Angeles, guests wearing faerie ears and wings watched fire breathers and acrobats. A German edition came out on the same day, with Spanish and French editions following on Wednesday.
Maas has sold 75 million books in 40 languages, according to AFP. The first novel in the series, published in 2015, has spent 92 consecutive weeks on the New York Times paperback bestseller list.
The series is published by Bloomsbury. A seventh novel is due on 12 January 2027, NBC News reported.

stories.head: Randa Abdel-Fattah accepts invitation to 2027 Adelaide Writers' Week
stories.say: Author Randa Abdel-Fattah has accepted an invitation to Adelaide Writers' Week in 2027, after her removal from this year's line-up led to a boycott and cancellation.
stories.stand: Festival organisers confirmed her place as they unveiled 2027 highlights; a Jewish community group opposes the invitation.
body: The Palestinian-Australian author Randa Abdel-Fattah has accepted an invitation to appear at Adelaide Writers' Week in 2027, ABC News reported. Festival artistic director Matthew Lutton confirmed her acceptance as 2027 Adelaide Festival highlights were unveiled.

In January 2026 the festival board removed her from that year's programme, citing her past statements. Writers boycotted the event, the 2026 Writers' Week was cancelled, and director Louise Adler and board members resigned.
The Festival Corporation later apologised to Abdel-Fattah and invited her back. New Writers' Week director Rosemarie Milsom said she supported her inclusion.
Norman Schueler of the Jewish Community Council of South Australia opposes the invitation. Premier Peter Malinauskas said the decision was entirely a matter for the festival board.

stories.head: British Library opens its Agatha Christie exhibition on Friday
stories.say: The British Library's Agatha Christie exhibition opens on Friday, fifty years after her death, with her typewriter, her exam notes and an Orient Express-style carriage.
stories.stand: The show runs until 20 June 2027, and its lead curator calls it the biggest UK exhibition on Christie's writing in almost 25 years.
body: Agatha Christie: A World of Mystery opens at the British Library in London on 30 October and runs until 20 June 2027. It marks 50 years since Christie's death.

The library says the show has more than 100 items from its own collection, the Christie Archive Trust and other lenders, some never displayed before. They include her 1917 pharmaceutical exam notes and her 1937 Remington typewriter.

The exhibition is arranged in 5 sections, including a dispensary and an Orient Express-inspired train carriage. Lead curator Lucy Rowland called it the biggest UK exhibition celebrating Christie's writing in almost 25 years.
A companion book edited by Martin Edwards and Lucy Rowland accompanies the show.

stories.head: Hobart replaces toppled Crowther statue with a garden and bronze ring
stories.say: Hobart has replaced the toppled statue of colonial surgeon William Crowther with a native garden inside a bronze ring, inscribed with texts including one on William Lanne.
stories.stand: Crowther is widely believed to have stolen Lanne's skull; vandals cut his statue down in 2024 shortly before a ruling backed its removal.
body: The City of Hobart has unveiled a permanent replacement for the statue of William Crowther in Franklin Square. The plinth now holds a native garden inside a bronze ring carrying three inscribed texts.
Crowther was a 19th-century surgeon and politician. Most historians agree he broke into a morgue and stole the skull of Aboriginal man William Lanne, ABC News reported.
Vandals cut the bronze statue down at the ankles in mid-2024, hours before a tribunal upheld the council's decision to remove it. The restored statue remains in council storage.
Lord Mayor Anna Reynolds said the project gives a fuller picture of the city's history. Councillor Louise Elliot opposed it, and 4 protesters held signs at the unveiling.

stories.head: Bronze Age defences with six towers found at Spain's La Almoloya
stories.say: Archaeologists say a defensive system with at least six towers guarded La Almoloya, a 4,000-year-old El Argar settlement on a cliff-ringed hilltop in south-east Spain.
stories.stand: Excavation directors from the Autonomous University of Barcelona say the walls reach up to 7 metres thick at the main entrance.
body: Archaeologists have found a monumental defensive system with at least six towers at La Almoloya, a Bronze Age settlement near Pliego in Murcia, Arkeonews reported. The wall is about 4,000 years old.
The work is led by the ASOME research group at the Autonomous University of Barcelona. Excavation directors Vicente Lull and Rafael Micó described the finds to El País, according to Arkeonews.

The walls reach up to 7 metres thick at the main entrance, although the dig covered only 11 square metres. The hilltop settlement belonged to the El Argar culture and was already protected by steep cliffs.

The Murcia regional government said in 2025 that the dig, begun in May that year, had uncovered two new sections of defensive wall. Regional heritage director Patricio Sánchez called La Almoloya one of the great Argaric sites.

stories.head: Milwaukee Brewers win first World Series title by beating Rays
stories.say: The Milwaukee Brewers beat the Tampa Bay Rays four-one in Game 5 on Wednesday, winning the World Series four games to one for the first title in the club's history.
stories.stand: Rookie Cooper Pratt drove in the first run and Jacob Misiorowski pitched 5 2/3 scoreless innings at Tropicana Field.
body: The Milwaukee Brewers won the World Series for the first time on Wednesday. They beat the Tampa Bay Rays 4-1 in Game 5 at Tropicana Field in St Petersburg, Florida, taking the series 4-1.

Cooper Pratt, a 22-year-old rookie, gave Milwaukee the lead in the second inning against Rays starter Drew Rasmussen. Starter Jacob Misiorowski allowed two hits over 5 2/3 scoreless innings before leaving with cramp. Trevor Megill closed out the win.

CBS News reported that Pratt set a World Series rookie record with six straight hits, and Jackson Chourio set a five-game series record with 11 hits. Tampa Bay's only run came from a Chandler Simpson double in the ninth.
It was only the Brewers' second World Series. They lost the 1982 series to the St Louis Cardinals in seven games. Manager Pat Murphy is 67. The Rays are now 0-3 in World Series appearances.

stories.say: Liverpool and Chelsea drew one-all at Anfield on Wednesday, with both goals from penalties, before Liverpool won the shootout six-five after Wesley Fofana's miss.
stories.stand: Morgan Rogers and Cody Gakpo scored penalties three minutes apart before Liverpool edged a long shootout at Anfield.
body: Liverpool knocked Chelsea out of the Carabao Cup on Wednesday night. The fourth-round tie at Anfield finished 1-1, and Liverpool won the shootout 6-5.

Morgan Rogers put Chelsea ahead from the penalty spot in the 40th minute after Ryan Gravenberch brought down Moises Caicedo. Cody Gakpo levelled with a penalty in the 43rd minute after a Fofana handball.
In the shootout Valentin Barco missed for Chelsea, while Konstantinos Tsimikas missed and Mike Penders saved from Gravenberch for Liverpool. Wesley Fofana's miss ended the contest.
Liverpool will face Bournemouth in the quarter-finals.

stories.head: Bayern coach Vincent Kompany leaves hospital after collapse
stories.say: Bayern Munich coach Vincent Kompany left hospital on Wednesday, five days after collapsing at training, with sporting chief Max Eberl blaming meningeal irritation.
stories.stand: Eberl said Kompany will rest and take medication, and no date has been set for his return to the touchline.
body: Bayern Munich head coach Vincent Kompany was discharged from hospital on Wednesday. He collapsed at the club's training ground on Friday while watching the second team train.

Sporting chief Max Eberl told German broadcaster ARD the collapse was caused by meningeal irritation. He said Kompany was "doing well" and would now rest and take medication. Kompany, 40, had earlier been ill with a virus.

No return date has been set. Assistant Aaron Danks has led the team to a 3-1 league win at Freiburg and a 6-1 German Cup win over Magdeburg. Bundesliga leaders Bayern host Borussia Dortmund on Saturday.

stories.stand: Russo now has 23 goals in the competition, and the win lifted Arsenal to second in the league-phase table.

Russo scored in the 29th and 66th minutes, then converted a 79th-minute penalty won by Caitlin Foord. It was her first Champions League hat-trick.

stories.stand: Chinese state media had suspended talks with the club, and Chinese brands have ended deals with the France forward.
body: Real Madrid issued a statement on Wednesday apologising "to the Chinese people" for offence caused by comments from Kylian Mbappé. The club said it respects China's history, culture and citizens.

In a video, Mbappé had joked about a meme putting his face on a man he called a "Chinese dictator". He apologised on Tuesday. La Liga president Javier Tebas also apologised and met China's ambassador to Spain.
Goal reported that China Media Group, which owns CCTV, had suspended all discussions with the club until a public apology. Al Jazeera said brands Dongpeng and Mengniu cut ties with Mbappé.
China's foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said Beijing took Mbappé's apology seriously.

Perez, 36, will make his 300th grand prix start at the Mexico City Grand Prix on Sunday. He said he was "fully committed for the next three years".

body: England head coach John Mitchell has made six changes for Friday's match against the USA in New Jersey. It is England's final WXV Global Series game.

Flo Robinson makes her first England start at scrum-half, alongside Holly Aitchison at fly-half. Claudia Moloney-MacDonald, Tatyana Heard, Mackenzie Carson and Maud Muir also come in. Meg Jones captains the side.
Ellie Kildunne is again among the replacements. Sky Sports said back-to-back defeats by Canada ended England's 41-Test unbeaten run.
Mitchell said the aim was "to start this next phase strongly", with six months until the Six Nations.

stories.head: New Zealand Rugby keeps Super Rugby Pacific and NPC, eyes player movement
stories.say: New Zealand Rugby has confirmed Super Rugby Pacific and the fourteen-team NPC as its men's competitions, and says it is open to talks on player movement and a salary cap.
stories.stand: The union plans to merge Super Rugby and provincial operations in five cities from 2028, subject to a final board decision.
body: New Zealand Rugby (NZR) has confirmed Super Rugby Pacific and the NPC as the country's two men's competitions. The NPC will stay at 14 teams.
NZR said Super Rugby and provincial union operations in the same five cities would be consolidated. Changes are expected from 2028, but a final board decision is still to come.

Chief executive Steve Lancaster said NZR was "open to working on" player movement, a competition-wide salary cap and centralising commercial assets. Those talks will involve Rugby Australia, the players' association and the clubs.
NZR said it aims to cut sport-wide costs by 5% and achieve a $20m annual improvement from 2028.
